turns.t: Hello there. Before we start, can I just check who I have? Is it Mr Alfred Dunmore, and I have you down for this morning at ten?
That's me. Dunmore, Alfred. Though I don't know what all the fuss is about, I told her it wasn't worth the bus fare.
Good morning, doctor. I'm Beatriz, I look after Mr Dunmore. It was me who made the appointment, because he wouldn't.
Thank you, Beatriz, I'm glad you did. So, Mr Dunmore, tell me in your own words why you're here today.
Honestly, it's only the hiccups. I'd have left it, they're a nuisance, that's all.
The hiccups. Right. I'm glad to have you in anyway, and I'd like to hear Beatriz's side too. Beatriz, what made you worry?
They keep coming back and he won't make a fuss, so I thought I'd better. I heard him up in the night through the wall, at three in the morning.
You've ears like a bat. I was just having a glass of water.
Mr Dunmore, a glass of water in the middle of the night is a perfectly sensible thing to do. Let me ask the main thing I'm checking. Have you been vomiting at all?
No, no vomiting. My stomach is as good as it's ever been.
No vomiting, good. That is exactly what I hoped to hear.
He also won't let me carry his bag, he says he can manage, even when the bus is packed.
I can carry my own bag, thank you. It's no great thing, Beatriz.
That's quite a good sign of independence. I'm not worried by that. Now, can I say what I'm thinking, so you both know where we are?
If you must.
I'm not going to do a lot of tests or give you any tablets today. I'd like you to try a few simple things at home first, and I'd like to see how you get on.
What things? I'm not standing on my head, I tell you that.
Nothing like that. Sipping cold water slowly, or swallowing a teaspoon of sugar, are the two I'd start with. Some people find that holding their breath for ten seconds or so helps.
My mother used to have us breathe into a paper bag.

A paper bag can work for some people too, as long as it's gentle and you stop if you feel lightheaded. So, to repeat, small sips of cold water, a teaspoon of sugar, and holding your breath for a few seconds.
That's all? You've no medicine for it?
No medicine for now. I'd rather see if the simple things do the job. If I prescribed something today, it might cause more bother than the hiccups do.
I've no objection to that. I've enough tablets in my life already, if you can call it a life.
Don't say that. You were singing along to the radio on Saturday.
Beatriz is right, and that sounds like a good sign. Now, is there anything you want to ask me before we finish?
Only whether I can have my cup of tea. I don't want to be told off for the tea.
Have your tea, but let it cool a little first, very hot drinks can set them off for some people.
Cool tea. That's a crime.
A small one. I'd like to see you again in a week, just to make sure things have settled. Beatriz, can you book him in with the front desk on the way out?
Of course. I'll do it before we go, and I'll write it on the kitchen calendar so he can't pretend he forgot.
Perfect. So that's cold sips, a teaspoon of sugar, a few seconds of held breath, and back to see me in a week.
Back to see you in a week. I heard you the first time, doctor, I'm not deaf.
I know you're not. You've been very patient with all of us today.
Well, thank you. And thank you, Beatriz, though I'd never admit it at home.
I know, I know. Come on, Mr Dunmore, let's get you some breakfast on the way home.

clinical_actions.description: Try sips of cold water, a teaspoon of sugar and holding the breath for a few seconds; let hot drinks cool
